newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.N. says Angolan rebel army has disbanded.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Angolan rebel army has disbanded.

text.p: U.N. peacekeepers in Angola said on Saturday the 20-year-old UNITA rebel army had practically disbanded as required by a peace plan, opening the way for a united country.
UNITA agreed in a 1994 accord with the Marxist government it had fought for two decades to dismantle its army gradually and merge some soldiers into a new, united Angolan force.

A spokesman for UNAVEM, the United Nations mission in Angola that ends in February, said by Friday some 70,000 rebel soldiers and police had entered 15 demilitarisation camps in the former Portuguese colony.

"UNAVEM considers that UNITA has fulfilled all military tasks required of it," he said in a statement sent to Reuters in Johannesburg, despite some worries about deserters, absconders and unaccounted-for military hardware.

"In spite of the reservations expressed, all obstacles to completing the formation of the Angolan Armed Forces and the extension of the state administration throughout the national territory have been removed," the statement added.
Nine UNITA generals have already been absorbed into the national army.
But observers say the peace process has been difficult, UNITA's disarming reluctant and political progress even slower.

UNITA (the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola), led by Jonas Savimbi and once backed by the United States and South African, still controls large stretches of the country, including diamond mines that help fill the party's coffers.
Despite rich mineral reserves, Angola's economy is in tatters after the civil war that started when the Portuguese abruptly quit in the mid-1970s and was then stoked by superpower Cold War rivalry.

The U.N. Angola Verification Mission, numbering 7,000 troops and military observers, will start leaving when the final extension of its mandate, approved by the Security Council on Wednesday, runs out on February 28.
Currently the largest U.N. peacekeeping mission, it will have overseen Angola's transition for two years.

Wednesday's resolution urged the government to avoid offensive operations beyond those needed for law and order in areas UNITA had occupied. Both sides were called on to redouble efforts to clear millions of mines.

Savimbi and Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos, whose MPLA forces were backed in the 1970s by Cuban troops, were urged to meet inside Angola soon to establish a government of national unity and reconciliation.
Recent attempts to arrange a summit between the two men have failed, despite intervention by South African President Nelson Mandela and other regional leaders.
